title: Estius: some acts of pagans are not sins but imperfectly good
source_text: XXVIII. Quam sententiam amplectitur Estius in secundum sententiarum Distinctione quadragesima prima paragrapho tertio. Ibi enim asserit quasdam infidelium actiones non tantum non esse peccata, sed & moraliter, licet imperfecte, bonas. Et notat hoc in loco a se infidelem non dici Judaeum aut haereticum, tametsi revera talis fidem non habeat, propterea quod fides integrae virtutis sit nomen, sed paganum, seu Ethnicum, qui ne unius quidem Dei, in quem suas actiones referre possit, cognitionem habeat. Censet enim ejusmodi infidelem aliquando operari ex naturali affectu, qui ex se ad bonum tendit, & actiones quasdam non in malum finem dirigere, sed ad bonum & finem ultimum in genere & confuse cognitum; quod sufficit ejus judicio ut non habeant rationem peccati. Nam sicut justi in hac vita non omnes suas actiones in Deum, quem habent pro fine ultimo, referunt, eas nimirum in quibus quotidie offendunt: ita nec necesse putat, ut injusti, licet infideles, referant omnes suas actiones, in illud quod prava voluntate statuerunt sibi summe diligendum. Quemadmodum enim concupiscentia interdum in justis surripit aliquos motus voluntatis, qui non referuntur in Deum, ut finem ultimum, ac ne referri quidem possunt; sic naturalis ad bonum instinctus aliquando, ex ejus mente, in infidelibus elicit actiones quasdam, quas homo non refert ad illud quod in particulari pro summo bono diligit, sed ad bonum & finem ultimum, saltem in genere, licet quis sit ille finis in particulari & distincte ignoretur.
pass_a_gloss: XXVIII. Which opinion Estius embraces on the second of the sentences Distinction forty-one paragraph three. For there he asserts that certain actions of unbelievers are not only not sins, but also morally, although imperfectly, good. And he notes that in this place by him an unbeliever is not called a Jew or a heretic, although in truth such a one does not have faith, because faith is the name of an entire virtue, but a pagan, or Heathen, who has knowledge not even of one God, to whom he could refer his actions. For he judges that such an unbeliever sometimes works from a natural affection, which of itself tends to good, and directs certain actions not to an evil end, but to good and to the last end known in general and confusedly; which suffices in his judgement that they do not have the character of sin. For as the just in this life do not refer all their actions to God, whom they have for their last end, namely those in which they offend daily: so he does not think it necessary that the unjust, although unbelievers, refer all their actions to that which by depraved will they have set for themselves to be loved supremely. For as concupiscence sometimes steals in the just some motions of the will, which are not referred to God, as the last end, and cannot even be referred; so the natural instinct to good sometimes, in his mind, elicits in unbelievers certain actions, which man does not refer to that which in particular he loves as the highest good, but to the good and the last end, at least in general, although what that end is in particular and distinctly be unknown.
pass_b_english: Estius takes this view on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 41, paragraph 3. He asserts there that some actions of unbelievers are not only not sins but are morally good, though imperfectly. He notes that by 'unbeliever' he does not mean a Jew or a heretic, even though such a person in truth has no faith, since faith is the name of a whole virtue. He means a pagan or heathen, who has no knowledge even of the one God to whom he might refer his actions.

He thinks such an unbeliever sometimes acts from a natural affection that of itself tends toward good, and directs some actions not to a bad end but to the good and to the last end, known in general and vaguely. In his judgement that is enough for them not to have the character of sin.

The righteous in this life do not refer all their actions to God, whom they hold as their last end; they do not so refer those in which they stumble daily. Likewise, he thinks, the unrighteous, even unbelievers, need not refer all their actions to what their corrupt will has set up as the thing to love above all.

Just as desire sometimes slips into the righteous some movements of the will that are not referred to God as last end, and cannot even be, so, on his view, the natural instinct for good sometimes draws from unbelievers actions that a man does not refer to what he loves in particular as the highest good. He refers them to the good and to the last end, at least in general, though he does not know what that end is in particular and distinctly.
